conclusion: You have two copies of the ε2 version of the APOE gene, which is rare: in the UK, about 6 in 1,000 people of European ancestry have it. The APOE gene comes in three common versions, called ε2, ε3 and ε4 (ε is the Greek letter epsilon; the versions are often called APOE2, APOE3 and APOE4). They differ from each other at two places in the gene, and everyone carries two versions, one from each parent. APOE helps carry cholesterol and other fats in the blood and the brain. This combination is linked with the lowest APOE-related risk of Alzheimer's disease that starts late in life. In large studies of people of European ancestry, people with two ε2 copies were less than half as likely to have the disease as people with two ε3 copies. Because so few people have this combination, the exact size is uncertain, and the effect was not clear in studies of Black and Hispanic people. Two ε2 copies can also lead to a blood-fat disorder in which cholesterol and another blood fat build up; doctors call it type III hyperlipoproteinaemia or dysbetalipoproteinaemia. Between about 1 in 10 and 1 in 3 people with two ε2 copies develop it, depending on how it is defined, usually together with something else such as excess weight or diabetes. It raises the risk of heart disease, shows up on a routine blood-fat test and can be treated, so this result is worth mentioning to your doctor.

You have one ε2 and one ε3 version of the APOE gene. In the UK, about 1 in 8 people of European ancestry have this combination. The APOE gene comes in three common versions, called ε2, ε3 and ε4 (ε is the Greek letter epsilon; the versions are often called APOE2, APOE3 and APOE4). They differ from each other at two places in the gene, and everyone carries two versions, one from each parent. APOE helps carry cholesterol and other fats in the blood and the brain. The ε2 version lowers the risk of Alzheimer's disease that starts late in life, and in people of European ancestry this is well established. One large estimate for people of European ancestry suggests that, among those who live to 85, about 5 in 100 men and 6 in 100 women who carry ε2 and no ε4 would develop Alzheimer's disease, against about 8 in 100 men and 10 in 100 women with two ε3 copies. The lowering was smaller in a large study of Black people and was not seen in studies of Hispanic or East Asian people. For any one person, age, other genes and health matter more than this result.

You have one ε2 and one ε4 version of the APOE gene. In the UK, about 2 to 3 in 100 people of European ancestry have this combination. The APOE gene comes in three common versions, called ε2, ε3 and ε4 (ε is the Greek letter epsilon; the versions are often called APOE2, APOE3 and APOE4). They differ from each other at two places in the gene, and everyone carries two versions, one from each parent. APOE helps carry cholesterol and other fats in the blood and the brain. The two versions pull in opposite directions: ε4 raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease that starts late in life and ε2 lowers it, but they do not cancel out. In large studies of people of European ancestry, this combination raised the risk, though less than one ε4 and one ε3 do. One large estimate for people of European ancestry suggests that, among those who live to 85, about 20 in 100 men and 27 in 100 women with this combination would develop Alzheimer's disease, against about 8 in 100 men and 10 in 100 women with two ε3 copies. This estimate is less certain than the others, because fewer people with this combination have been studied, and the increase was smaller or unclear in studies of Black and Hispanic people. Most people with this combination do not develop the disease. Doctors do not use an APOE result to predict Alzheimer's disease in people without symptoms. If a doctor ever considers the newer antibody medicines for Alzheimer's disease, which clear a protein called amyloid from the brain, your APOE type matters, because ε4 raises the risk of a common side effect of these medicines: swelling or small bleeds in the brain. A genetic counsellor can explain what this result means for you. Very rarely, the same DNA letters come instead from an uncommon version called ε1 together with ε3; a DNA file that does not record which letters came from the same parent cannot tell the two apart, and this report reads it as ε2/ε4.

Two ε4 copies carry the highest APOE-related risk of Alzheimer's disease that starts late in life, and this is well established. Nearly everyone with two copies shows the brain changes of Alzheimer's disease in medical tests by their mid-60s, but not everyone develops symptoms. If symptoms do come, they tend to start earlier, at about 65 on average in a large 2024 study. The increase is smaller in studies of Black and Hispanic people. Because this result can weigh on people, a genetic counsellor or doctor is the right person to put it in context.
